title: The Baghdad Battery: electricity in a clay jar
excerpt: A 13-centimeter clay jar found in 1936 near Baghdad holds a copper cylinder and an iron rod. Was it an electric battery from 2000 years ago or just a container for storing scrolls?
content:
A clay jar about 13 centimeters long, a copper cylinder, and an iron rod held in place with bitumen. That is all that appeared in 1936 in Khujut Rabu, near Baghdad, and it is enough to fuel decades of debate. The topic reached the radio through a special on Milenio 3 (Cadena SER), and at foro3d.com we think it is a perfect case for separating facts from fantasy.

What König said and what archaeologists say 🏺

Two years after the discovery, Wilhelm König, an assistant at the Iraq Museum, published that this could be a galvanic cell, perhaps used to gild silver by means of electricity. Replicas with grape juice, vinegar, or lemon generate a weak current, around half a volt per jar. But no galvanized object from that period is known in the region, the gilding that König believed was electrical was probably done with mercury, and the copper tube was not watertight. The jar appears to be from the Sasanian period, and other similar ones contained remains of scrolls.

A battery that perhaps only held prayers 📜

The most widely accepted explanation is less electrifying: it was used to store sacred or magical texts. Even so, the legend lives on, and the whereabouts of many of these pieces have been unknown since the Iraq War of 2003. Do you have any information about these jars or about the experiments with replicas? Tell us about it.
